newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish court delays ruling on extradition to China.
newsitem.headline: Polish court delays ruling on extradition to China.

text.p: A Warsaw court on Monday delayed indefinitely giving an opinion on whether Poland can extradite two members of China's Mongolian minority, wanted by Beijing for embezzlement.
Human rights activists say Mandugeqi, 52 and his 42-year-ld wife Yinge, could face the death penalty in China.
The court asked China to provide more information on the case within one month, the couple's lawyer said.
It also asked the Polish Interior Ministry for details of the progress of a bid by the couple for asylum, and the human rights group Amnesty International for a report on human rights in China.
"This is a very good decision," lawyer Wojciech Hermelinski told Reuters, adding that the request to London-based Amnesty was particularly significant.
Mandugeqi and Yinge were detained in Warsaw in August on the basis of an Interpol notice and have since been held in jail pending a decision on China's extradition request.
Yinge was asked to comment on Beijing's extradition bid before the couple were escorted back to jail.
"It is political," she hastily told Reuters.

Polish prosecutors have asked the court to rule on whether they can be surrendered if China agrees not to impose higher penalties than they would face for similar offences in Poland and specifically not the death sentence.
China would also have to promise to try them only for the charges specified in its extradition request.
If the court says extradition is possible, the final decision rests with prosecutor-general Leszek Kubicki.
Mandugeqi, 52, said he had been jailed in China for eight years on political charges and had since worked for China's security services, an observer at the closed session of the court said.
The observer quoted him as saying he had gone to Mongolia in 1993 with thousands of dollars received from the Chinese authorities, and had then failed to return to the country.

Hermelinski earlier said they faced imprecise allegations of embezzlement, failing to repay borrowed money from banks and individuals and of not paying for goods, involving a total of 17.5 million yuan ($2.1 million).
The couple deny the allegations, saying they had repaid almost all they owed and assets they had left in China covered any outstanding sums.
Hermelinski argues the couple should not be extradited as the Chinese allegations would be treated in Poland as a civil rather than a criminal case.

He and human rights campaigners also say economic crimes are punished in China by shooting or long terms in labour camps and Beijing in 1995 broke a promise to Thailand not to execute someone extradited under similar circumstances.

"We know that the death penalty is applied to 68 various crimes in China. The broad charge against Mandugeqi of financial embezzlement, which he denies...incurs death," said Amnesty International representative Boguslaw Stanislawski.
He said Amnesty, though not familiar with Mandugeqi's case, opposed any extradition that might lead to a breach of rights.
Poland and China do not have an extradition treaty, although the issue was raised by Kubicki in Beijing this month.
